Validate with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload ssh' (the unit is named 'ssh' on Ubuntu).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Check that the ssh package is installed with the following command:

# sudo dpkg -l | grep openssh
ii openssh-client 1:7.6p1-4ubuntu0.1 amd64 secure shell (SSH) client, for secure access to remote machines
ii openssh-server 1:7.6p1-4ubuntu0.1 amd64 secure shell (SSH) server, for secure access from remote machines
```


#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without protection of the transmitted information, confidentiality and integrity may be compromised because unprotected communications can be intercepted and either read or altered.

This requirement applies to both internal and external networks and all types of information system components from which information can be transmitted (e.g., servers, mobile devices, notebook computers, printers, copiers, scanners, and facsimile machines). Communication paths outside the physical protection of a controlled boundary are exposed to the possibility of interception and modification.

Protecting the confidentiality and integrity of organizational information can be accomplished by physical means (e.g., employing physical distribution systems) or by logical means (e.g., employing cryptographic techniques). If physical means of protection are employed, then logical means (cryptography) do not have to be employed, and vice versa.

Alternative physical protection measures include PDS. PDSs are used to transmit unencrypted classified National Security Information (NSI) through an area of lesser classification or control. Since the classified NSI is unencrypted, the PDS must provide adequate electrical, electromagnetic, and physical safeguards to deter exploitation.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-255906 · UBTU-18-010421 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system SSH server must be configured to use only FIPS-validated key exchange algorithms.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-255906r991554_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000250-GPOS-00093 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140), SSH Remote Administration |
| CCI | CCI-000068 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-17 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-17 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-17 (2) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer SSH server must be configured to use only FIPS-validated key exchange algorithms.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SSH*: Secure Shell: an encrypted way to control a computer remotely by typing commands.
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/ssh/sshd_config | KexAlgorithms | ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -i kexalgorithms /etc/ssh/sshd_config
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo sshd -T | grep -i '^KexAlgorithms '
```

Expected: kexalgorithms ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256 (the effective value sshd is using).

**How it works:** Ubuntu provides FIPS 140-validated modules through Ubuntu Pro: 'pro enable fips-updates' (or 'fips'), then reboot into the FIPS kernel. Verify with 'cat /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled' (expect 1). sshd ciphers, MACs and key exchange algorithms are set explicitly in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, because Ubuntu has no RHEL-style system-wide crypto-policies.

**Also related (SSH Remote Administration):** sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and, on 22.04 and later, drop-ins in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf, which are included at the top of the main file so their values take precedence (first value wins). Validate with 'sshd -t', check the effective configuration with 'sshd -T | grep -i <keyword>', then 'systemctl reload ssh' (the unit is named 'ssh' on Ubuntu).

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older Java code, legacy VPN or SSH clients). FIPS packages require an Ubuntu Pro subscription and a reboot into the FIPS kernel, and the FIPS kernel may lag behind the general kernel's hardware enablement. Test interoperating systems before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the SSH server is configured to use only FIPS-validated key exchange algorithms:

     $ sudo grep -i kexalgorithms /etc/ssh/sshd_config
     KexAlgorithms ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256

If "KexAlgorithms" is not configured, is commented out, or does not contain only the algorithms "ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256" in exact order, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the SSH server to use only FIPS-validated key exchange algorithms by adding or modifying the following line in "/etc/ssh/sshd_config":

     KexAlgorithms ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256

Restart the "sshd" service for changes to take effect:

     $ sudo systemctl restart sshd
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without cryptographic integrity protections provided by FIPS-validated cryptographic algorithms, information can be viewed and altered by unauthorized users without detection.

The system will attempt to use the first algorithm presented by the client that matches the server list. Listing the values "strongest to weakest" is a method to ensure the use of the strongest algorithm available to secure the SSH connection.

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption; T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000068**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality of remote access sessions.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (2) · Rev 4: AC-17 (2) · Rev 3: AC-17 (2)

```text
# egrep '(Permit(.*?)(Passwords|Environment))' /etc/ssh/sshd_config

PermitEmptyPasswords no
PermitUserEnvironment no

If "PermitEmptyPasswords" or "PermitUserEnvironment" keywords are not set to "no", are missing completely, or they are commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to allow the SSH daemon to not allow unattended or automatic login to the system.

Add or edit the following lines in the "/etc/ssh/sshd_config" file:

PermitEmptyPasswords no
PermitUserEnvironment no

In order for the changes to take effect, the SSH daemon must be restarted.

# sudo systemctl restart sshd.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Failure to restrict system access to authenticated users negatively impacts Ubuntu operating system security.

**Threat & control context:** SSH is the primary remote administration channel on Linux and therefore a high-value target. Hardening reduces the attack surface: no root or empty-password logins, no host-based trust (rhosts) or user environment injection, strict file-mode checks, idle-session termination, and approved cryptography only. These settings support AC-17 (Remote Access), AC-12, IA-2 and SC-8. Also check authorized_keys sprawl and key lifecycle, which no STIG setting fully covers.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1021.004 Remote Services: SSH; T1110 Brute Force; T1098.004 Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys; T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

**Legacy IDs:** SV-109955, V-100851

### V-219315 · UBTU-18-010425 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system, for PKI-based authentication, must validate certificates by constructing a certification path (which includes status information) to an accepted trust anchor.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-219315r958448_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000066-GPOS-00034 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000185, CCI-001991 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (2) (b) (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (2) (a), IA-5 (2) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (2) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer , for PKI-based authentication, must validate certificates by constructing a certification path (which includes status information) to an accepted trust anchor.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf | cert_policy | ca,signature,ocsp_on; |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep use_pkcs11_module /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf | awk '/pkcs11_module opensc {/,/}/' /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf | grep cert_policy | grep ca
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*cert_policy\b' /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf
```

Expected: cert_policy = ca,signature,ocsp_on;

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses libpam-pkcs11 and opensc-pkcs11 for CAC/PIV login: a pam_pkcs11.so line in /etc/pam.d/common-auth, certificate mapping and OCSP/CRL policy in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf, and DoD CA certificates installed under /etc/ssl/certs (or /usr/local/share/ca-certificates followed by 'update-ca-certificates').

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Ubuntu operating system, for PKI-based authentication, had valid certificates by constructing a certification path to an accepted trust anchor.

Check which pkcs11 module is being used via the use_pkcs11_module in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf and then ensure "ca" is enabled in "cert_policy" with the following command:

# sudo grep use_pkcs11_module /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf | awk '/pkcs11_module opensc {/,/}/' /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf | grep cert_policy | grep ca

cert_policy = ca,signature,ocsp_on;

If "cert_policy" is not set to "ca", or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system, for PKI-based authentication, to validate certificates by constructing a certification path to an accepted trust anchor.

Determine which pkcs11 module is being used via the use_pkcs11_module in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf and ensure "ca" is enabled in "cert_policy".

Add or update the "cert_policy" to ensure "ca" is enabled:

cert_policy = ca,signature,ocsp_on;

If the system is missing an "/etc/pam_pkcs11/" directory and an "/etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf", find an example to copy into place and modify accordingly at "/usr/share/doc/libpam-pkcs11/examples/pam_pkcs11.conf.example.gz".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without path validation, an informed trust decision by the relying party cannot be made when presented with any certificate not already explicitly trusted.

A trust anchor is an authoritative entity represented via a public key and associated data. It is used in the context of public key infrastructures, X.509 digital certificates, and DNSSEC.

When there is a chain of trust, usually the top entity to be trusted becomes the trust anchor; it can be, for example, a Certification Authority (CA). A certification path starts with the subject certificate and proceeds through a number of intermediate certificates up to a trusted root certificate, typically issued by a trusted CA.

This requirement verifies that a certification path to an accepted trust anchor is used for certificate validation and that the path includes status information. Path validation is necessary for a relying party to make an informed trust decision when presented with any certificate not already explicitly trusted. Status information for certification paths includes certificate revocation lists or online certificate status protocol responses. Validation of the certificate status information is out of scope for this requirement.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000066-GPOS-00034, SRG-OS-000384-GPOS-00167

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000185**: For public key-based authentication, validate certificates by constructing and verifying a certification path to an accepted trust anchor including checking certificate status information.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (2) (b) (1) · Rev 4: IA-5 (2) (a) · Rev 3: IA-5 (2)
- **CCI-001991**: The information system, for PKI-based authentication, implements a local cache of revocation data to support path discovery and validation in case of inability to access revocation information via the network.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (2) (d) · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** V-100853, SV-109957

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must map the authenticated identity to the user or group account for PKI-based authentication.

Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**


**How it works:** Ubuntu uses libpam-pkcs11 and opensc-pkcs11 for CAC/PIV login: a pam_pkcs11.so line in /etc/pam.d/common-auth, certificate mapping and OCSP/CRL policy in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf, and DoD CA certificates installed under /etc/ssl/certs (or /usr/local/share/ca-certificates followed by 'update-ca-certificates').

**Also related (Account Lifecycle Management):** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Ubuntu operating system has the "libpam-pkcs11" package installed, by running the following command:

     # dpkg -l | grep libpam-pkcs11

If "libpam-pkcs11" is not installed, this is a finding.

Check if use_mappers is set to pwent in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf file
     # grep use_mappers /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf
     use_mappers = pwent

If "use_mappers" is not found, or is not set to "pwent", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install libpam-pkcs11 package on the system.

Set use_mappers=pwent in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf

If the system is missing an "/etc/pam_pkcs11/" directory and an "/etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf", find an example to copy into place and modify accordingly at "/usr/share/doc/libpam-pkcs11/examples/pam_pkcs11.conf.example.gz".
```

The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without the use of multifactor authentication, the ease of access to privileged functions is greatly increased.

Multifactor authentication requires using two or more factors to achieve authentication.

Factors include:

2) something a user has (e.g., cryptographic identification device, token); and
3) something a user is (e.g., biometric).

A privileged account is defined as an information system account with authorizations of a privileged user.

Network access is defined as access to an information system by a user (or a process acting on behalf of a user) communicating through a network (e.g., local area network, wide area network, or the internet).

The DOD CAC with DOD-approved PKI is an example of multifactor authentication.

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Using an authentication device, such as a CAC or token that is separate from the information system, ensures that even if the information system is compromised, that compromise will not affect credentials stored on the authentication device.

A privileged account is defined as an information system account with authorizations of a privileged user.

Remote access is access to DoD nonpublic information systems by an authorized user (or an information system) communicating through an external, non-organization-controlled network. Remote access methods include, for example, dial-up, broadband, and wireless.

This requirement only applies to components where this is specific to the function of the device or has the concept of an organizational user (e.g., VPN, proxy capability). This does not apply to authentication for the purpose of configuring the device itself (management).

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Ubuntu operating system accepts Personal Identity Verification (PIV) credentials.

Check that the "opensc-pcks11" package is installed on the system with the following command:

# dpkg -l | grep opensc-pkcs11

ii opensc-pkcs11:amd64 0.15.0-1Ubuntu1 amd64 Smart card utilities with support for PKCS#15 compatible cards

If the "opensc-pcks11" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to accept Personal Identity Verification (PIV) credentials.

Install the "opensc-pkcs11" package using the following command:

# sudo apt-get install opensc-pkcs11
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The use of PIV credentials facilitates standardization and reduces the risk of unauthorized access.

DoD has mandated the use of the CAC to support identity management and personal authentication for systems covered under Homeland Security Presidential Directive (HSPD) 12, as well as making the CAC a primary component of layered protection for national security systems.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001953**: Accept Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (12) · Rev 4: IA-2 (12) · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** V-100861, SV-109965

### V-219321 · UBTU-18-010436 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must only allow the use of DoD PKI-established certificate authorities for verification of the establishment of protected sessions.

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must only allow the use of DoD PKI-established certificate authorities for verification of the establishment of protected sessions.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses libpam-pkcs11 and opensc-pkcs11 for CAC/PIV login: a pam_pkcs11.so line in /etc/pam.d/common-auth, certificate mapping and OCSP/CRL policy in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf, and DoD CA certificates installed under /etc/ssl/certs (or /usr/local/share/ca-certificates followed by 'update-ca-certificates').

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the directory containing the root certificates for the Ubuntu operating system only contains certificate files for DoD PKI-established certificate authorities by iterating over all files in the '/etc/ssl/certs' directory and checking if, at least one, has the subject matching "DOD ROOT CA".

If none is found, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Add at least one DOD certificate authority to the '/usr/local/share/ca-certificates' directory, then run the 'update-ca-certificates' command.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Untrusted Certificate Authorities (CA) can issue certificates, but they may be issued by organizations or individuals that seek to compromise DoD systems or by organizations with insufficient security controls. If the CA used for verifying the certificate is not a DoD-approved CA, trust of this CA has not been established.

The DoD will only accept PKI-certificates obtained from a DoD-approved internal or external certificate authority. Reliance on CAs for the establishment of secure sessions includes, for example, the use of SSL/TLS certificates.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-219322 · UBTU-18-010437 · CAT III: Pam_Apparmor must be configured to allow system administrators to pass information to any other Ubuntu operating system administrator or user, change security attributes, and to confine all non-privileged users from executing functions to include disabling, circumventing, or altering implemented security safeguards/countermeasures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-219322r958702_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00122 |
| Topic | Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-002165, CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 (4), AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 (4), AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd), Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** Pam_Apparmor must be configured to allow system administrators to pass information to any other this computer administrator or user, change security attributes, and to confine all non-privileged users from executing functions to include disabling, circumventing, or altering implemented security safeguards/countermeasures.

**Why it matters:** Behind the sign-in screen is a chain of checks: the password is right, the account isn't locked, the password isn't expired, and so on. This rule makes sure every check in that chain is present and in the correct order, like making sure every guard at a multi-checkpoint entrance is at their post.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | libpam-apparmor | Installed |
| Service | systemd | apparmor.service | enable |
| Service | systemd | apparmor.service | start |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep -i apparmor
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl status apparmor.service | grep -i active
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l libpam-apparmor 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package libpam-apparmor is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled apparmor.service; systemctl is-active apparmor.service
```

Expected: Expect enabled / active.

**How it works:** Ubuntu's PAM stacks are /etc/pam.d/common-auth, common-account, common-password and common-session. They are regenerated by 'pam-auth-update' from profiles in /usr/share/pam-configs/, so persistent changes belong in a custom profile there or must be re-checked after package updates. SSSD (if used) is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf (mode 0600, owned by root).

**Operational impact:** PAM mistakes can lock everyone out, including root. Test changes from a second, still-open root session, and keep console access available.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the Ubuntu operating system is configured to allow system administrators to pass information to any other Ubuntu operating system administrator or user.

Check that "Pam_Apparmor" is installed on the system with the following command:

# dpkg -l | grep -i apparmor

ii libpam-apparmor 2.10.95-0Ubuntu2.6

If the "Pam_Apparmor" package is not installed, this is a finding.

Check that the "AppArmor" daemon is running with the following command:

# systemctl status apparmor.service | grep -i active

If something other than "Active: active" is returned, this is a finding.

Note: Pam_Apparmor must have properly configured profiles. All configurations will be based on the actual system setup and organization. See the "Pam_Apparmor" documentation for more information on configuring profiles.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to allow system administrators to pass information to any other Ubuntu operating system administrator or user.

Install "Pam_Apparmor" (if it is not installed) with the following command:

# sudo apt-get install libpam-apparmor

Enable/Activate "Apparmor" (if it is not already active) with the following command:

# sudo systemctl enable apparmor.service

Start "Apparmor" with the following command:

# sudo systemctl start apparmor.service

Note: Pam_Apparmor must have properly configured profiles. All configurations will be based on the actual system setup and organization. See the "Pam_Apparmor" documentation for more information on configuring profiles.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When discretionary access control policies are implemented, subjects are not constrained with regard to what actions they can take with information for which they have already been granted access. Thus, subjects that have been granted access to information are not prevented from passing (i.e., the subjects have the discretion to pass) the information to other subjects or objects. A subject that is constrained in its operation by Mandatory Access Control policies is still able to operate under the less rigorous constraints of this requirement. Thus, while Mandatory Access Control imposes constraints preventing a subject from passing information to another subject operating at a different sensitivity level, this requirement permits the subject to pass the information to any subject at the same sensitivity level. The policy is bounded by the information system boundary. Once the information is passed outside the control of the information system, additional means may be required to ensure the constraints remain in effect. While the older, more traditional definitions of discretionary access control require identity-based access control, that limitation is not required for this use of discretionary access control.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00122, SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00123, SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00124, SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-0012

**Threat & control context:** PAM and SSSD define how every Linux authentication decision is made. Misordered or optional modules silently bypass controls such as faillock, pwquality and pwhistory. Credential caching lifetimes trade availability against revocation latency, so a revoked account keeps working offline until its cache expires. These settings support IA-2, IA-5(13) (expiration of cached authenticators), AC-7, AC-9 (previous logon notification) and AC-10 (concurrent session control).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002165**: Enforce organization-defined discretionary access control policies over defined subjects and objects.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 (4) · Rev 4: AC-3 (4) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** V-100867, SV-109971

### V-219323 · UBTU-18-010441 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must be configured to use AppArmor.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-219323r958804_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-001764 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd), Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to use AppArmor.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | apparmor | Installed |
| Service | systemd | apparmor.service | enable |
| Service | systemd | apparmor.service | start |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep apparmor
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l apparmor 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package apparmor is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled apparmor.service; systemctl is-active apparmor.service
```

Expected: Expect enabled / active.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system prevents program execution in accordance with local policies.

Check that apparmor is installed and active by running the following command:

# dpkg -l | grep apparmor

If the "apparmor" package is not installed, this is a finding.

#systemctl is-active apparmor.service

active

If "active" is not returned, this is a finding.

#systemctl is-enabled apparmor.service

enabled

If "enabled" is not returned, then this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install "Apparmor" (if it is not installed) with the following command:

# sudo apt-get install apparmor

# sudo systemctl enable apparmor.service

Start "Apparmor" with the following command:

# sudo systemctl start apparmor.service

Note: Apparmor must have properly configured profiles for applications and home directories. All configurations will be based on the actual system setup and organization and normally are on a per role basis. See the "Apparmor" documentation for more information on configuring profiles.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Control of program execution is a mechanism used to prevent execution of unauthorized programs. Some operating systems may provide a capability that runs counter to the mission or provides users with functionality that exceeds mission requirements. This includes functions and services installed at the operating system level.

Some of the programs, installed by default, may be harmful or may not be necessary to support essential organizational operations (e.g., key missions, functions). Removal of executable programs is not always possible; therefore, establishing a method of preventing program execution is critical to maintaining a secure system baseline.

Methods for complying with this requirement include restricting execution of programs in certain environments, while preventing execution in other environments; or limiting execution of certain program functionality based on organization-defined criteria (e.g., privileges, subnets, sandboxed environments, or roles).

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

**Legacy IDs:** SV-109973, V-100869

Install and enable it with 'apt-get install ufw' and 'ufw enable', set default-deny with 'ufw default deny incoming', and allow only the required services ('ufw allow <port>/<proto>', or 'ufw limit ssh' for rate limiting). Review with 'ufw status verbose'.

```text
apparmor module is loaded.
17 profiles are loaded.
17 profiles are in enforce mode.
 /sbin/dhclient
 /usr/bin/lxc-start
 ...
0 processes are in complain mode.
0 processes are unconfined but have a profile defined.

If the defined profiles do not match the organization's list of authorized software, this is a finding.
```

```text
# sudo apt-get install apparmor

# sudo systemctl start apparmor.service

Note: Apparmor must have properly configured profiles for applications and home directories. All configurations will be based on the actual system setup and organization and normally are on a per role basis. See the "Apparmor" documentation for more information on configuring profiles.
```

Some of the programs, installed by default, may be harmful or may not be necessary to support essential organizational operations (e.g., key missions, functions). Removal of executable programs is not always possible; therefore, establishing a method of preventing program execution is critical to maintaining a secure system baseline.

Methods for complying with this requirement include restricting execution of programs in certain environments, while preventing execution in other environments; or limiting execution of certain program functionality based on organization-defined criteria (e.g., privileges, subnets, sandboxed environments, or roles).

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation; T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001774**: Employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy to allow the execution of authorized software programs on the system.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (5) (b) · Rev 4: CM-7 (5) (b) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-219325 · UBTU-18-010444 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must uniquely identify interactive users.

| Field | Value |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must uniquely identify interactive users.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
awk -F ":" 'list[$3]++{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the Ubuntu operating system contains no duplicate User IDs (UIDs) for interactive users.

Check that the Ubuntu operating system contains no duplicate UIDs for interactive users with the following command:

# awk -F ":" 'list[$3]++{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd

If output is produced, and the accounts listed are interactive user accounts, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Edit the file "/etc/passwd" and provide each interactive user account that has a duplicate User ID (UID) with a unique UID.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To assure accountability and prevent unauthenticated access, organizational users must be identified and authenticated to prevent potential misuse and compromise of the system.

Organizational users include organizational employees or individuals the organization deems to have equivalent status of employees (e.g., contractors). Organizational users (and processes acting on behalf of users) must be uniquely identified and authenticated to all accesses, except for the following:

1) Accesses explicitly identified and documented by the organization. Organizations document specific user actions that can be performed on the information system without identification or authentication; and

2) Accesses that occur through authorized use of group authenticators without individual authentication. Organizations may require unique identification of individuals in group accounts (e.g., shared privilege accounts) or for detailed accountability of individual activity.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000104-GPOS-00051, SRG-OS-000121-GPOS-00062

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000804**: Uniquely identify and authenticate non-organizational users or processes acting on behalf of non-organizational users.

### V-219326 · UBTU-18-010445 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must disable account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) after 35 days of inactivity.

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | n/a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-4 e |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-4 e |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) after 35 days of inactivity.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep INACTIVE /etc/default/useradd
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) are disabled after 35 days of inactivity with the following command:

Check the account inactivity value by performing the following command:

# sudo grep INACTIVE /etc/default/useradd

INACTIVE=35

If "INACTIVE" is not set to a value 0<[VALUE]<=35, or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to disable account identifiers after 35 days of inactivity since the password expiration.

Run the following command to change the configuration for adduser:

# sudo useradd -D -f 35

Note: DoD recommendation is 35 days, but a lower value is acceptable. The value "0" will disable the account immediately after the password expires.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inactive identifiers pose a risk to systems and applications because attackers may exploit an inactive identifier and potentially obtain undetected access to the system. Owners of inactive accounts will not notice if unauthorized access to their user account has been obtained.

Ubuntu operating systems need to track periods of inactivity and disable application identifiers after 35 days of inactivity.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000795**: The organization manages information system identifiers by disabling the identifier after an organization-defined time period of inactivity.

### V-219327 · UBTU-18-010447 · CAT III: The Ubuntu operating system must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-219327r958508_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000123-GPOS-00064 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-001682 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
chage -l <temporary_account_name> | grep -i "account expires"
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify temporary accounts have been provisioned with an expiration date of 72 hours.

For every existing temporary account, run the following command to obtain its account expiration information:

     $ sudo chage -l <temporary_account_name> | grep -i "account expires"

Verify each of these accounts has an expiration date set within 72 hours.
If any temporary accounts have no expiration date set or do not expire within 72 hours, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the operating system to expire temporary accounts after 72 hours with the following command:

     $ sudo chage -E $(date -d +3days +%Y-%m-%d) <temporary_account_name>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Temporary accounts are privileged or nonprivileged accounts that are established during pressing circumstances, such as new software or hardware configuration or an incident response, where the need for prompt account activation requires bypassing normal account authorization procedures. If any inactive temporary accounts are left enabled on the system and are not either manually removed or automatically expired within 72 hours, the security posture of the system will be degraded and exposed to exploitation by unauthorized users or insider threat actors.

Temporary accounts are different from emergency accounts. Emergency accounts, also known as "last resort" or "break glass" accounts, are local logon accounts enabled on the system for emergency use by authorized system administrators to manage a system when standard logon methods are failing or not available. Emergency accounts are not subject to manual removal or scheduled expiration requirements.

The automatic expiration of temporary accounts may be extended as needed by the circumstances but it must not be extended indefinitely. A documented permanent account should be established for privileged users who need long-term maintenance accounts.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001682**: Automatically remove or disable emergency accounts after an organization-defined time period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)

**Legacy IDs:** SV-109981, V-100877

### V-219328 · UBTU-18-010448 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system default filesystem permissions must be defined in such a way that all authenticated users can only read and modify their own files.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-219328r991590_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00228 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer default filesystem permissions must be defined in such a way that all authenticated users can only read and modify their own files.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | UMASK | 077 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i "umask" /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*UMASK\b' /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: UMASK = 077

**How it works:** Check mode and ownership with 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' and fix them with 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp'. Find unowned files with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup'. Default permissions for new files come from UMASK in /etc/login.defs. 'dpkg --verify' highlights packaged files that have changed.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Ubuntu operating system defines default permissions for all authenticated users in such a way that the user can only read and modify their own files.

Check that the Ubuntu operating system defines default permissions for all authenticated users with the following command:

# grep -i "umask" /etc/login.defs

UMASK 077

If the "UMASK" variable is set to "000", this is a finding with the severity raised to a CAT I.

If the value of "UMASK" is not set to "077", "UMASK" is commented out or "UMASK" is missing completely, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the system to define the default permissions for all authenticated users in such a way that the user can only read and modify their own files.

Edit the "UMASK" parameter in the "/etc/login.defs" file to match the example below:

UMASK 077
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Setting the most restrictive default permissions ensures that when new accounts are created they do not have unnecessary access.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

**Legacy IDs:** SV-109983, V-100879

### V-219329 · UBTU-18-010449 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must provision temporary user accounts with an expiration time of 72 hours or less.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-219329r958364_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000002-GPOS-00002 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-000016 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must provision temporary user accounts with an expiration time of 72 hours or less.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
chage -l system_account_name | grep expires
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Ubuntu operating system expires temporary user accounts within 72 hours or less.

For every existing temporary account, run the following command to obtain its account expiration information.

# sudo chage -l system_account_name | grep expires

Password expires : Aug 07, 2019
Account expires : Aug 07, 2019

Verify each of these accounts has an expiration date set within 72 hours of accounts' creation.
If any temporary account does not expire within 72 hours of that account's creation, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If a temporary account must be created configure the system to terminate the account after a 72 hour time period with the following command to set an expiration date on it. Substitute "system_account_name" with the account to be created.

# sudo chage -E $(date -d "+3 days" +%F) system_account_name
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If temporary user accounts remain active when no longer needed or for an excessive period, these accounts may be used to gain unauthorized access. To mitigate this risk, automated termination of all temporary accounts must be set upon account creation.

Temporary accounts are established as part of normal account activation procedures when there is a need for short-term accounts without the demand for immediacy in account activation.

If temporary accounts are used, the Ubuntu operating system must be configured to automatically terminate these types of accounts after a DoD-defined time period of 72 hours.

To address access requirements, the Ubuntu operating system may be integrated with enterprise-level authentication/access mechanisms that meet or exceed access control policy requirements.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000016**: Automatically remove or disable temporary and emergency accounts after an organization-defined time-period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)

**Legacy IDs:** SV-109985, V-100881

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the assigned home directory of all local interactive users on the Ubuntu operating system exists.

Check the home directory assignment for all local interactive non-privileged users with the following command:

$ sudo awk -F: '($3>=1000)&&($7 !~ /nologin/){print $1, $3, $6}' /etc/passwd

smithj 1001 /home/smithj

Note: This may miss interactive users that have been assigned a privileged User ID (UID). Evidence of interactive use may be obtained from a number of log files containing system logon information.

Check that all referenced home directories exist with the following command:

$ sudo pwck -r

user 'smithj': directory '/home/smithj' does not exist

If any home directories referenced in "/etc/passwd" are returned as not defined, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Create home directories to all local interactive users that currently do not have a home directory assigned. Use the following commands to create the user home directory assigned in "/etc/ passwd":

Note: The example will be for the user smithj, who has a home directory of "/home/smithj", a User ID (UID) of "smithj", and a Group Identifier (GID) of "users assigned" in "/etc/passwd".

$ sudo mkdir /home/smithj
$ sudo chown smithj /home/smithj
$ sudo chgrp users /home/smithj
$ sudo chmod 0750 /home/smithj
```

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** All local interactive user home directories must have mode 0750 or less permissive.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | 0750 /home/smithj |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
ls -ld $(awk -F: '($3>=1000)&&($7 !~ /nologin/){print $6}' /etc/passwd)
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo stat -c '%a %U %G %n' /home/smithj
```

Expected: Mode/owner/group must match: chmod 0750 /home/smithj.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** Check mode and ownership with 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' and fix them with 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp'. Find unowned files with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup'. Default permissions for new files come from UMASK in /etc/login.defs. 'dpkg --verify' highlights packaged files that have changed.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the assigned home directory of all local interactive users has a mode of "0750" or less permissive with the following command:

Note: This may miss interactive users that have been assigned a privileged User Identifier (UID). Evidence of interactive use may be obtained from a number of log files containing system logon information.

$ sudo ls -ld $(awk -F: '($3>=1000)&&($7 !~ /nologin/){print $6}' /etc/passwd)

drwxr-x--- 2 smithj admin 4096 Jun 5 12:41 smithj

If home directories referenced in "/etc/passwd" do not have a mode of "0750" or less permissive, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Change the mode of interactive user’s home directories to "0750". To change the mode of a local interactive user’s home directory, use the following command:

Note: The example will be for the user "smithj".

$ sudo chmod 0750 /home/smithj
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Excessive permissions on local interactive user home directories may allow unauthorized access to user files by other users.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-219330 · UBTU-18-010500 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must be configured to use TCP syncookies.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-219330r958528_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000142-GPOS-00071 |
| Topic | Network Stack Hardening, Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-001095 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-5 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-5 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-5 (2) |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to use TCP syncookies.

**Why it matters:** These settings change how the computer handles network traffic at a low level, for example ignoring suspicious "take a detour" messages and not answering "who is this?" broadcasts that attackers can fake. It's like a mail room that refuses packages with forged return addresses and won't hand mail to anyone who just shouts a name.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.
- *sudo*: A Linux command that lets an approved user temporarily act with administrator power.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.conf | net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies | 1 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* | grep -v '#'
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -rs '^[[:space:]]*net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/ /run/sysctl.d/ /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/ /usr/lib/sysctl.d/ /lib/sysctl.d/
```

Expected: Every match must set 1. Conflicting values in other files are a finding.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, set these with sysctl drop-ins in /etc/sysctl.d/ (net.ipv4.conf.all/default.accept_redirects = 0, send_redirects = 0, accept_source_route = 0, ip_forward = 0, rp_filter = 1, tcp_syncookies = 1, icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1, and IPv6 equivalents). Apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Both 'all' and 'default' must be set so that new interfaces inherit the values. DNS resolvers are set through NetworkManager or /etc/resolv.conf.

**Also related (Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features):** On Ubuntu, the equivalents are disabling Apport crash reporting ('systemctl disable --now apport'), the 'ubuntu-report' and popularity-contest data collection, MOTD news ('ENABLED=0' in /etc/default/motd-news), and GNOME online accounts if they're not approved.

**Operational impact:** Hosts that legitimately route (VPN concentrators, container and Kubernetes nodes, libvirt hosts) need IP forwarding and must document the exception. Disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS requires working DNS for all name lookups.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Ubuntu operating system is configured to use TCP syncookies.

Check the value of TCP syncookies with the following command:

# sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1

If the value is not "1", this is a finding.

Check the saved value of TCP syncookies with the following command:

# sudo grep -i net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/* | grep -v '#'

If no output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to use TCP syncookies, by running the following command:

# sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1

If "1" is not the system's default value then add or update the following line in "/etc/sysctl.conf":

net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** DoS is a condition when a resource is not available for legitimate users. When this occurs, the organization either cannot accomplish its mission or must operate at degraded capacity.

Managing excess capacity ensures that sufficient capacity is available to counter flooding attacks. Employing increased capacity and service redundancy may reduce the susceptibility to some DoS attacks. Managing excess capacity may include, for example, establishing selected usage priorities, quotas, or partitioning.

**Threat & control context:** Host network-stack defaults favor interoperability over safety. Accepting ICMP redirects or source-routed packets lets an on-path attacker reroute traffic. IP forwarding turns a host into an unintended router between security zones. Multicast name resolution (LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS) is trivially poisoned to capture NTLM hashes. Reverse-path filtering and SYN cookies blunt spoofing and resource-exhaustion attacks. These settings support SC-5, SC-7 (boundary protection) and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1498 Network Denial of Service; T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001095**: Manage capacity, bandwidth, or other redundancy to limit the effects of information flooding types of denial-of-service attacks.  
  Rev 5: SC-5 (2) · Rev 4: SC-5 (2) · Rev 3: SC-5 (2)

**Legacy IDs:** SV-109987, V-100883
